strengths: The paper addresses a genuinely important problem: goal-agnostic evaluation of LM agents without hand-designed benchmarks. Adapting empowerment to high-dimensional, sparse, text-based state/action spaces is a natural but unexplored direction, and EELMA is plausibly the first method to estimate effective empowerment from multi-turn text interactions.

The validation methodology is sound: in Gridworld and Tower of Hanoi, where direct estimation via empirical conditional probabilities is tractable, EELMA estimates are shown to converge to and strongly correlate with ground truth (Figure 3, Figure 9), which is the right way to validate an MI estimator before deploying it in WebArena.

The ablation studies (CoT, memory length, closed vs. open model families, model scale) are reasonably extensive and yield interpretable findings, e.g., large empowerment drops without CoT and monotone gains with memory.

The WebArena authentication case study is a compelling demonstration that state-action conditional empowerment can flag pivotal, safety-relevant events (gaining authenticated access) without reward annotations, with sensible follow-up analysis of username vs. password typing effects.

Robustness is evaluated in a meaningful way: paraphrase-based natural-language variability experiments (Appendix I) and comparison against a prompt-only LLM estimator (Appendix J, which overestimates by 10-25x) both strengthen the case for an experience-grounded estimator.
Reproducibility is comparatively good: anonymous code is provided, and the appendices include detailed architectures, hyperparameters, training configurations, prompts, seeds, and compute budgets.
weaknesses: The theoretical contribution is largely borrowed. The empowerment-to-expected-return connection (Appendix A.2) restates Myers et al. (2025) under the same strong assumptions. Notably, the Boltzmann-rationality assumption about the LLM agent is almost certainly violated in practice, so the claimed link between empowerment and goal-averaged performance is essentially empirical, not principled; the paper should be clearer about this gap.

The headline correlation claims rest on very few data points. In WebArena, domain-wise correlations (Rs=0.83-0.94) are computed over only three models per domain (Figure 7B, Table 3), and the agent-variation correlations in Figure 6 are over roughly 8 closed-source or ~10 open-source configurations. No confidence intervals or significance tests are reported for these correlations, so 'strongly correlates with average task performance' is weakly supported statistically.

The estimated quantities show pathologies that are not adequately discussed: mean state-action empowerment of -0.127 bits for invalid authentication (Figure 8) is impossible for a true mutual information and indicates substantial estimator bias; large seed-level variance is visible in Table 3 (e.g., std of 0.0532-0.0633 bits on quantities of order 0.4-0.7).

There is an apparent inconsistency between the robustness narrative and the results: Table 1 and its surrounding text claim EELMA remains accurate under NL variability, but Figure 11 shows mean empowerment for EELMA-NL collapsing to 0.025 bits vs. 0.295 bits ground truth in Hanoi (and even below GT-NL at 0.082), which contradicts the 'preserves method ranking' and 'remains close' claims for at least one domain.

Empowerment is measured under the agent's own policy (E depends on pi_LM), so the metric partially conflates agent behavior with environment structure. A weak agent that never explores cannot exhibit high empowerment even if the environment permits it; the paper does not discuss this circularity or how it affects interpretation as a 'capability' metric. This may underlie the flat empowerment-reward relationship in the Shopping domain, which is acknowledged but left unexplained.

Writing and presentation contain enough errors to impede careful reading: e.g., 'PODMP' for POMDP, 'authentification', 'memroy', 'rweard', 'COMPAREMENT', mismatched descriptions of Gridworld vs. ToH moves in E.1, unclear conditioning notation in Equations 1-3 (I(a_t; s* | a) vs. | s_t), and an 'r' label floating above Figure 13.

The reward metric choice matters and is somewhat favorable to the method: correlations are with mean discounted reward rather than success rate, and the paper itself notes o3 matches GPT-4o on success rate but scores lower on discounted reward; a correlation analysis against success rate would test robustness of the proxy claim.

EELMA requires environment-specific training on collected trajectories (embedding MLP plus encoders retrained per environment/domain), so the practical cost of the 'scalable' evaluation relative to simply running task-based evaluation is not clearly quantified.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuine problem: scalable, goal-agnostic evaluation of LM agents beyond hand-crafted benchmarks. Framing capability via empowerment (mutual information between actions and future states) is a principled angle.

Validation is sensible in structure: the method is first checked against directly computable ground truth in small, tractable environments (Gridworld, Tower of Hanoi), where EELMA closely matches direct estimation (Fig. 3), before being applied to the more realistic WebArena setting.

The robustness experiment on natural-language paraphrasing (Table 1, Appendix I) is a well-motivated and useful addition, showing that embedding-based estimation degrades less than direct counting under linguistic variability, and the prompt-only LLM baseline comparison (Appendix J) strengthens the case for the learned estimator.

The authentication case study (Sec. 5, Fig. 8) is an interesting demonstration that state-action empowerment can flag pivotal, security-relevant transitions without reward labels, with reasonable statistical treatment (Welch's t-tests).
The paper is reasonably transparent about compute, hyperparameters, prompts, and provides anonymized code, supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty. The core estimator is a direct port of the contrastive successor-representation mutual-information estimator of Myers et al. (2025) to text embeddings (Eq. 4, 5-7 essentially restate their results). The main contribution is applying an existing method to a new domain, which weakens the claim of a 'novel information-theoretic estimator'.

Theoretical motivation is weak and the assumptions are implausible for the claimed setting. Appendix A.2 imports a lower bound requiring uniform Dirichlet-distributed rewards over states, ergodicity, and Boltzmann rationality of the LM agent. These assumptions do not plausibly hold for goal-conditioned LM agents in WebArena, and the paper does not discuss how far the empirical correlation could be expected to carry given this gap.

Potential circularity/confounding is not addressed. EELMA is trained on the very trajectories whose (discounted) rewards are then correlated with estimated empowerment. An agent that succeeds on more goals explores more diverse states, so high empowerment may simply be a byproduct of task success and trajectory coverage rather than an independent measure of capability. The paper provides no control experiment (e.g., estimating empowerment on failure-only trajectories) to disentangle this.

The central empirical evidence for the WebArena proxy claim is thin: correlations are computed over only 3 models x 4 domains (12 points, Fig. 7B), and one of four domains (Shopping) shows a flat relationship, which the authors explain away post hoc. This partially undercuts the headline claim that empowerment 'strongly correlates with average task performance'.

Negative empowerment values are reported (e.g., -0.127 bits for invalid authentication actions, Fig. 8/10) without comment. Mutual information is non-negative; negative values indicate the InfoNCE lower bound is loose/biased in this regime, which deserves analysis since the method is precisely advocated for distinguishing such actions.

Presentation quality is below bar for a main-track submission: numerous typos and grammatical errors ('COMPARENEMENT', 'authentification', 'enviornment', 'PODMP', 'corrsponding'), a broken sentence in Appendix J ('EELMA, and Direct Estimation are .'), inconsistent/undefined notation (Eq. 1 conditions on an undefined variable 'a'; the discounted sum indexed by t inside an expectation over tau is confusing; Lemma 1 mixes s* and s+_gamma), and Figure 6's axes/labels are hard to parse.

Scalability and practicality of the 'general-purpose metric' claim are questionable. A separate EELMA model must be trained per environment (and effectively per domain, with environment-specific prompts and augmented goal sets), so the method does not yet provide the scalable, open-ended evaluation the introduction promises.

The 'goal-agnostic' framing is weakened by the requirement to generate diverse random goals (via LLMs) to obtain sufficiently varied trajectories for training; the estimator is thus more goal-dependent than claimed.

Statistical rigor is uneven: Spearman correlations on ~12 points are reported without confidence intervals; some t-tests treat non-independent action-level samples as independent; and several ablation effects (e.g., CoT '99% decrease' from 0.19 to 0.01 bits) rest on single configurations without variance reporting.

strengths: Novel and interesting research direction: the paper is, to my knowledge, the first to attempt estimating empowerment (mutual information between actions and future states) directly from multi-turn text trajectories of LM agents, adapting the contrastive successor-representation MI estimator of Myers et al. (2025) to language spaces.

Careful validation in controlled settings: in Gridworld and Tower of Hanoi, where direct (MLE-based) empowerment estimation is tractable, EELMA estimates converge to ground truth (Fig. 3, Fig. 9) and correctly rank scenarios of increasing optionality; state-action conditional empowerment discriminates valid from invalid actions with statistical significance (Fig. 4).

The robustness study on natural-language variability (Table 1, Appendix I) is a valuable addition: it shows that direct estimation collapses under paraphrase while EELMA remains accurate, which is precisely the property needed for text-based environments.

A broad ablation suite (CoT, memory length, closed vs. open models of varying scale) with reported correlations between empowerment and mean discounted reward, plus comparison against a prompt-only LLM estimator baseline showing 10-25x overestimation (Appendix J), strengthens the empirical case.

The authentication case study in modified WebArena is a creative demonstration of reward-free detection of pivotal behavior, and the paper releases code and provides detailed prompt/hyperparameter documentation in appendices.
An honest limitations section acknowledges that more options do not always equal more power and that indirect forms of influence are not captured.
weaknesses: The central conceptual tension is underexamined: EELMA estimates on-policy MI between action and future state under the agent's own policy. A deterministic, highly capable agent has low action entropy and thus potentially near-zero MI, whereas a stochastic but incompetent agent could receive moderate MI. The paper uses classical channel capacity as motivation (optionality) but estimates a policy-dependent quantity; the relationship between these two notions, and what the resulting 'effective empowerment' actually measures for near-deterministic LLM agents, is not analyzed. This is glossed over rather than resolved.

The theoretical connection to capability (Appendix A.2) is essentially restated from Myers et al. (2025), with strong assumptions (uniform Dirichlet rewards over states, ergodicity, Boltzmann rationality of the LM agent) that are transparently violated by LLM agents acting greedily with CoT. The empirical empowerment-performance correlation therefore carries most of the evidential weight, and it is correlational: both quantities are computed from the same trajectories and are driven by the same underlying model competence, so confounding (e.g., a generally better model both succeeds more and visits more states) is not ruled out. No causally-informative control (e.g., fixing the policy while varying the environment) is offered.

Missing baselines: the only quantitative baseline is direct estimation (which fails under NL variability) and a prompt-only LLM. Simple proxies such as unique-state count, action entropy, or embedding-based state diversity could plausibly explain the same correlations and are not compared; this weakens the claim that the MI-based quantity specifically is the useful signal.

Known limitations of InfoNCE-based MI estimation (bias, temperature sensitivity, bound looseness - the paper itself cites Rusak et al., 2025) are not quantified for this setting. Seed variability in Table 3 is substantial (std up to 0.05-0.06 bits), which is the same order as some between-model differences the paper interprets (e.g., o3 shopping_admin 0.362 vs. o3 gitlab 0.383).

The WebArena evidence is thin: correlations are computed over only 3 models x 3-4 domains (roughly 9-12 points), the Shopping domain shows a flat relationship (explained post-hoc), and the discounted rewards are all small (0.015-0.069), making rank correlations fragile. The strong claims in the abstract ('strongly correlates', 'general-purpose metric') overreach what this sample size supports.

The safety-monitoring claim is oversold relative to the evidence: that valid password typing yields higher empowerment than invalid attempts is close to a foregone conclusion, since successful authentication trivially unlocks a larger reachable state space. One case study on one model (GPT-4o with 1-step memory, which was the only configuration that succeeded at all) does not establish a scalable anomaly-monitoring tool.

Presentation issues: numerous typos and inconsistencies ('COMPAREMENT', 'PODMP', 'authentification', 'rweard', incoherent sentence 'EELMA, and Direct Estimation are .'), Eq. (1) conditions on 'a' where it should presumably be s_t, the E.1 Gridworld task description erroneously contains Tower of Hanoi bullet points, and Figure 7A labels discounted rewards at ~0.004-0.006 that do not match Table 2 values (~0.03-0.07). These suggest insufficient polish for a main-track submission.

Reproducibility concerns: headline results depend on closed-source models (GPT-4o, o3, Claude) whose trajectories cannot be regenerated exactly, and no ablation over the choice of text embedding model is provided, so the sensitivity of all conclusions to the specific encoder (e5-small-v2 / jina-v2) is unknown.

strengths: Novel and well-motivated direction: EELMA is presented as the first empowerment estimator for text-based LM agents, addressing a genuine gap since classical counting-based estimators fail under observation redundancy and linguistic variability.

Careful validation against ground truth: In Gridworld and Tower of Hanoi, EELMA estimates are compared against direct computation of conditional mutual information (state-level Spearman R_s = 0.80–0.94), and robustness to LLM-induced natural-language paraphrasing is tested against a direct-estimation baseline that degrades badly (Table 1).

Exceptionally honest treatment of failure modes: The paper explicitly analyzes when empowerment is uninformative — the flat reward-empowerment relation in WebArena Shopping, Qwen's jailbreaking inflating state diversity (Figure 12), and the τ-bench retail inversion at floor performance — and the Limitations section is substantive rather than perfunctory.

Useful baseline comparisons: Against diversity-based metrics (Table 5) and prompt-only LLM estimators (Appendix J, 10–25x overestimation), the paper shows empowerment is the strongest task-agnostic correlate among the tested signals.

Good reproducibility: hyperparameters, prompt templates, model versions, seeds, compute resources, and code availability are all documented; negative empowerment values and estimator bias are explained in Appendix G.4.
The authentication case study (Figure 9/11) is a compelling demonstration of detecting pivotal, reward-free actions without manual annotation.
weaknesses: The central hypothesis (empowerment proxies general capability) is supported with considerably weaker evidence in the realistic settings than the abstract implies: the pooled WebArena correlation is only R_s = 0.39 over 16 model-domain points, Shopping shows no relation, and τ-bench retail inverts. With N=6 points in τ-bench, the reported correlations are statistically fragile; 'strongly correlates' in the abstract overstates the results.

The theoretical justification is entirely borrowed from Myers et al. (2024) and rests on strong assumptions (uniform reward distribution, ergodicity, Boltzmann rationality) whose plausibility for LLM agents with hand-prompted goals is not examined; the paper treats the theorem as motivation rather than testing its assumptions.

The estimator's approximation E ≈ Ê requires E[C1(ot,at) − C2(ot)] ≈ 0, which is admittedly unguaranteed; the difference of two InfoNCE lower bounds is not itself a lower bound on the CMI, and no formal error analysis or bias quantification is provided beyond empirical plots. Negative estimates and the Figure 13 anomaly (EELMA 'outperforming' ground truth in Gridworld) indicate the estimator's accuracy is inconsistent across settings.

Empowerment is policy-dependent: the metric is estimated under the agent's own trajectory distribution, so it partly measures exploration/diversity of behavior rather than capability, as the authors' own jailbreaking and retail-domain examples demonstrate. The paper does not offer a fix, only boundary conditions.

The 'goal-agnostic' claim is partially undermined by the methodology: trajectory collection requires diverse goal-directed prompting and, in WebArena, LLM-generated goals to obtain enough data; the metric never sees goals, but the data pipeline does. Data requirements (800–1600 trajectories per environment) and the need for per-environment EELMA training limit scalability, which is acknowledged but not resolved.

NL robustness is mixed: EELMA-NL degrades severely in Tower of Hanoi (0.025 vs. 0.223 bits for structured EELMA), suggesting sensitivity to compositional state descriptions; the paper flags this but the realistic-environment validation (WebArena, τ-bench) cannot disentangle this encoder limitation.

Minor presentation issues: empty 'Code available:' URL, typos ('Texual' in Figure 2, 'curernt'), and some claims (e.g., 5% overhead) count only EELMA training, not the substantial trajectory-generation cost.

strengths: The paper tackles a genuinely important problem: scalable, goal-agnostic evaluation of LM agents beyond hand-crafted benchmarks, and empowerment is a well-motivated information-theoretic candidate for this.

The EELMA estimator is validated against ground-truth empowerment in controlled environments (Gridworld, Tower of Hanoi) with a principled direct-estimation baseline, showing reasonable tracking (Spearman 0.80-0.94) and robustness to linguistic variability where counting-based estimators fail (Table 1).

The paper is unusually honest about failure modes: the Qwen 'jailbreaking' inflation of empowerment on Reddit, the flat empowerment-performance relationship on Shopping, and the inversion in the tau-bench retail domain are all documented rather than hidden, and the Limitations section articulates when empowerment is and is not informative.
Reproducibility support is above average: full prompt templates, hyperparameters, architecture details, compute costs, and ablations over encoders and fine-tuning strategies (Appendices D-L).
The authentication case study is a nice demonstration that state-action-conditional empowerment can flag pivotal, security-relevant behaviors without task-specific annotation.
weaknesses: The central claim is overclaimed relative to the evidence. The abstract states empowerment 'strongly correlates with average task performance,' yet in the realistic WebArena setting the pooled Spearman correlation is only Rs = 0.39 (Table 5), and per-domain fits rest on just 4 model-domain points. The strongest correlations come from the controlled toy environments; the evidence in the settings that actually motivate the paper is mixed.

Sample sizes for the headline realistic-setting correlations are very small: 16 model-domain points for WebArena and 6 for tau-bench, with domain effects confounded into the pooled correlations. No confidence intervals or significance tests are reported for these correlations, and three of the four key domains/conditions exhibit flat or inverted relationships.

The theoretical framing (Appendix A.2) is essentially restated from Myers et al. (2024) and relies on assumptions - uniformly distributed rewards over states, ergodicity, and Boltzmann-rational agents - that are implausible for prompted LLM agents; the paper does not discuss how badly these assumptions are violated in WebArena or tau-bench, weakening the theoretical motivation for the empirical hypothesis.

The 'first empowerment estimator for text-based LM-agents' contribution claim is undercut by the paper's own citation of Ellis et al. (2025), which applies token-level empowerment to LLM agents (mentioned only in Appendix M).

Estimator bias is a real concern: negative empowerment estimates (e.g., -0.094 bits for valid actions in Figure 9, -0.127 in Figure 11) are acknowledged as variational-lower-bound artifacts, and the residual bias C1-C2 in Eq. 6 is 'not guaranteed' to vanish. This makes the absolute bit values difficult to interpret, yet several conclusions (e.g., 99% vs 65% CoT drops) are reported in absolute bits.

Presentation defects: the code link is literally empty in both the abstract ('Code available:') and Appendix D, Figure 2 contains a typo ('Texual Trajectories'), and the paper inconsistently reports trajectory-level vs action-level authentication statistics (0.268/-0.094 in text vs 0.365/-0.127 in Figure 11) in a way that initially reads as contradictory.

Some analyses feel underpowered or post hoc: the invalid-username comparison has only n=22 and is admitted as non-significant, and the Shopping-domain 'reasoning bottleneck' explanation is speculative with no direct evidence.

strengths: Novel and well-motivated problem: adapting empowerment estimation to text-based LM agents is a genuinely new direction, and EELMA is a sensible instantiation (text embeddings + InfoNCE-based MI estimation following Myers et al., 2024).

Strong validation methodology in controlled settings: Gridworld and Tower of Hanoi permit direct ground-truth empowerment computation, and EELMA is shown to track it closely (Spearman 0.80–0.94), including robustness tests under LLM-generated linguistic paraphrasing where direct estimation fails (Table 1).

Breadth of evaluation: textual games, WebArena across four domains, and τ-bench tool use; extensive ablations (CoT, memory, model scale, open vs. closed models), baseline comparisons against diversity metrics and a prompt-only LLM estimator (Appendix J), and architecture/encoder/fine-tuning sensitivity analyses (Appendices K, L).

Unusually honest treatment of failure modes: the paper itself documents where empowerment fails as a capability signal (Qwen jailbreaking inflating empowerment, flat Shopping-domain relation, τ-bench retail inversion at floor performance) and folds these into an explicit boundary-condition discussion in Section 6.
Good reproducibility support in the appendix: full prompt templates, environment configurations, hyperparameters, compute details, and an impact statement addressing dual-use concerns.
weaknesses: The central claim of 'strong correlation with average task performance' is overstated relative to the evidence: the pooled WebArena correlation is only Rs = 0.39 over 16 model-domain points, one of four WebArena domains shows a flat relation, τ-bench retail shows an inversion, and the headline r values (0.70–0.91) come from small-N ablation plots. The abstract does not convey these boundary conditions.

Potential circularity in the capability proxy: effective empowerment is computed under the agent's own policy, so more capable agents will by construction take more diverse, effective actions. The CoT/memory ablations in particular simultaneously change the behavior distribution and the performance, making it unclear how much of the correlation reflects genuine 'capability' versus behavioral diversity that correlates with capability.

The theoretical motivation relies on strong assumptions (uniform reward distribution over the state simplex, ergodicity, Boltzmann rationality of the LLM) that are patently unrealistic for LM agents; the paper leans on this theory to motivate the hypothesis but does not test the assumptions, and the result is largely imported from Myers et al. (2024).

Estimator validity is not fully established: the approximation E ≈ Ê requires the residual terms C1(ot, at) − C2(ot) to have small expectation, which is explicitly 'not guaranteed' for finite K; negative empowerment estimates arise in practice, and validation against ground truth is only possible in the same toy games where the method is later used to make claims—no independent validation of EELMA's accuracy in WebArena/τ-bench.

The claim of being 'the first empowerment estimator for text-based LM-agents' needs softening given concurrent/closely related work the authors themselves cite (e.g., Ellis et al., 2025 applying token-level empowerment for LLM agents).

Presentation issues reduce polish: the code availability link is empty in the submitted version, several typos ('Texual', 'curernt'), and some citations are imprecise (e.g., citing Du et al., 2020 and Jung et al., 2011 for high-dimensional intractability).
